checks.label: Security Patch Level
checks.command: SP=$(getprop ro.build.version.security_patch 2>/dev/null); if [ -z "$SP" ]; then echo "UNKNOWN no security_patch property"; else P=$(printf '%s' "$SP" | tr -d '-' | cut -c1-6); N=$(date +%Y%m); PY=$(( ${P%??} + 0 )); PM=$(( 1${P#????} - 100 )); NY=$(( ${N%??} + 0 )); NM=$(( 1${N#????} - 100 )); D=$(( (NY-PY)*12 + (NM-PM) )); if [ "$D" -lt 0 ]; then echo "FUTURE_SPL spl=$SP months_ahead=$(( -D ))"; elif [ "$D" -le 3 ]; then echo "RECENT spl=$SP months_old=$D"; elif [ "$D" -le 6 ]; then echo "AGING spl=$SP months_old=$D"; else echo "OUTDATED spl=$SP months_old=$D"; fi; fi
checks.description: Single authoritative answer to how old the device security patch level is. Reports months_old relative to the current month: RECENT at 3 months or less, AGING at 4 to 6, OUTDATED beyond 6, and FUTURE_SPL when the patch date is ahead of today, which no honest build produces and which spoofing tooling does. The arithmetic is integer YYYYMM subtraction and does not call 'date -d'. The earlier version did, and when 'date -d' was unavailable (toybox and busybox builds vary) it fell back to epoch 0, computed an age of roughly 20000 days and scored CRITICAL on a device with a perfectly current patch. This check replaces two other currency checks that answered the same question with different thresholds and different severities.
checks.remediation: Apply the vendor OTA. If FUTURE_SPL is reported, the patch level is forged: locate the spoofing module and treat the device as compromised.

checks.label: Third-Party App Stores
checks.description: Avoid non-Google app stores
checks.remediation: Uninstall third-party app stores. Run: pm uninstall <package_name> for each detected store.

checks.label: User-installed Apps
checks.description: Check how many user apps installed
checks.remediation: Review the list with pm list packages -3 and uninstall unnecessary apps: pm uninstall <package_name>.

checks.label: Unusual Files in /sdcard/
checks.description: Sensitive files in user-accessible storage
checks.remediation: Remove sensitive files from /sdcard/. Run: adb shell rm /sdcard/<filename> for each flagged file.

checks.label: Zygote Process Check
checks.description: Zygote process is core to Android app lifecycle
checks.remediation: If zygote is missing, the system is severely compromised. Reflash the factory firmware image immediately.

checks.label: Wi-Fi Direct Disabled (WFD)
checks.description: Wi-Fi Direct (WFD) package should be removed if unused
checks.remediation: Disable or uninstall the WFD package. Run: pm disable <wfd_package> or pm uninstall <wfd_package>.

checks.label: Auto System Update Enabled
checks.description: Auto updates improve patch consistency
checks.remediation: Enable auto updates. Run: adb shell settings put global auto_update_system 1.

checks.label: Kernel Hardening (PAN/UAO)
checks.command: if [ ! -e /proc/config.gz ]; then echo 'NOT_OBSERVABLE /proc/config.gz absent (CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC disabled)'; else K=$( (zcat /proc/config.gz 2>/dev/null || gzip -dc /proc/config.gz 2>/dev/null) | grep -cE '^CONFIG_ARM64_(PAN|UAO)=y' ); echo "PAN_UAO_COUNT=${K:-0}"; fi
checks.description: Privileged Access Never and User Access Override stop the kernel from dereferencing userspace pointers outside the accessor helpers, which blocks a large family of privilege escalation primitives. Both are compile-time kernel options, observable only through /proc/config.gz. That file requires CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC and is absent on the majority of production Android builds, so this check now reports NOT_OBSERVABLE explicitly instead of silently producing an empty result. NOT_OBSERVABLE is treated as passing because failing a device for the absence of evidence would be a false positive, not a finding.
checks.remediation: Where the kernel config is readable, confirm CONFIG_ARM64_PAN=y and CONFIG_ARM64_UAO=y. Where it is not, obtain the defconfig from the vendor kernel source drop for the exact build and verify there.

checks.label: World-Writable Directories
checks.description: World-writable directories in system
checks.remediation: Remove world-write permission. Run: chmod o-w <directory> for each flagged path (requires root/remount).

checks.label: SUID Binaries
checks.description: SUID binaries - review for privilege escalation
checks.remediation: Review each SUID binary. Remove the SUID bit from unnecessary ones: chmod u-s <binary> (requires remount).

checks.label: Exposed Unix Sockets
checks.description: Unix sockets - potential IPC attack vectors
checks.remediation: Review each socket owner and permissions. Restrict access with chmod 600 on sockets not needed by other users.

checks.label: Debugfs Mounted
checks.description: Debugfs mounted - kernel debug info exposed
checks.remediation: Unmount debugfs. Run: umount /sys/kernel/debug. Prevent at boot by removing debugfs from fstab.

checks.label: Executable Stack
checks.description: ASLR should be enabled
checks.remediation: Enable ASLR. Run: echo 2 > /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space. Persist via sysctl.conf.

checks.label: Ptrace Scope
checks.description: Ptrace restrictions (1+ recommended)
checks.remediation: Restrict ptrace. Run: echo 1 > /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope. Persist via sysctl.conf.

checks.label: Recent Kernel Crashes
checks.description: Recent kernel panics or fatal errors
checks.remediation: Investigate crash logs for root cause. Update the kernel or drivers if a known bug is identified.

checks.label: Application Crash Log
checks.description: Recent app crash logs (look for repeated exceptions)
checks.remediation: Review crash logs with: adb logcat -b crash. Update or reinstall repeatedly crashing applications.

checks.label: Kernel Stack Protector (Strong)
checks.command: if [ ! -e /proc/config.gz ]; then echo 'NOT_OBSERVABLE /proc/config.gz absent (CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC disabled)'; else (zcat /proc/config.gz 2>/dev/null || gzip -dc /proc/config.gz 2>/dev/null) | grep -E '^CONFIG_(CC_)?STACKPROTECTOR_STRONG=' | head -1 | grep . || echo STACKPROTECTOR_STRONG_ABSENT; fi
checks.description: The strong stack protector places a canary in every kernel function with a local array or address-taken local, so a stack buffer overflow is detected before the saved return address is used. It is a compile-time option observable only through /proc/config.gz, which needs CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC and is absent on most production Android builds. The check now reports NOT_OBSERVABLE rather than failing on absence of evidence, and matches both the modern CONFIG_STACKPROTECTOR_STRONG and the legacy CONFIG_CC_STACKPROTECTOR_STRONG spelling. This replaces an earlier version that ran zcat with no stderr redirect and scored CRITICAL from the resulting gzip error on every device lacking the file.
checks.remediation: Where the kernel config is readable, confirm CONFIG_STACKPROTECTOR_STRONG=y. Where it is not, verify against the vendor defconfig for the exact build.

checks.label: Pointer Authentication (PAC) CPU Support
checks.command: A=$(uname -m 2>/dev/null); C=$(grep -m1 -iE '^Features' /proc/cpuinfo 2>/dev/null); P=$(printf '%s' "$C" | grep -owE 'paca|pacg' | tr '\n' ' '); if [ "$A" != "aarch64" ]; then echo "NOT_ARM64 arch=${A:-unknown}"; elif [ -n "$P" ]; then echo "PAC_CPU_SUPPORTED features=$P"; else echo PAC_CPU_ABSENT; fi
checks.description: Pointer Authentication signs return addresses and function pointers with a hardware key, so an attacker who corrupts a saved return address cannot forge a valid signature. This defeats most classical ROP chains. The kernel advertises support in the /proc/cpuinfo Features list as 'paca' (address authentication) and 'pacg' (generic authentication). PAC is an ARMv8.3 feature present on essentially all ARM64 Android silicon from 2019 onward, so its absence on a modern device is a genuine hardening gap. This replaces an earlier version that read 'zcat /proc/config.gz' with no stderr redirect, which emitted a gzip error and scored CRITICAL on every device where that file is absent.
checks.remediation: PAC cannot be added in software. On ARMv8.3+ hardware, confirm the kernel is built with CONFIG_ARM64_PTR_AUTH=y and that userspace is compiled with -mbranch-protection=standard. On pre-ARMv8.3 silicon the only remedy is a hardware refresh.

checks.label: Memory Tagging (MTE)
checks.command: A=$(uname -m 2>/dev/null); C=$(grep -m1 -iE '^Features' /proc/cpuinfo 2>/dev/null); H=$(printf '%s' "$C" | grep -owE 'mte' | head -1); BC=$(getprop arm64.memtag.bootctl 2>/dev/null); DF=$(getprop persist.arm64.memtag.default 2>/dev/null); if [ "$A" != "aarch64" ]; then echo "NOT_ARM64 arch=${A:-unknown}"; elif [ -n "$H" ]; then echo "MTE_CPU_SUPPORTED bootctl=${BC:-unset} default=${DF:-unset}"; else echo "MTE_CPU_ABSENT bootctl=${BC:-unset} default=${DF:-unset}"; fi
checks.description: Memory Tagging Extension is an ARMv8.5 hardware feature that tags heap allocations and traps mismatched accesses, converting most heap overflow and use-after-free bugs into faults. Support is reported in the /proc/cpuinfo Features list as 'mte'; the arm64.memtag.bootctl and persist.arm64.memtag.default properties report whether Android is actually asking for it at boot. Informational because MTE requires ARMv8.5 silicon that most fleet hardware through 2026 does not have, so absence is a hardware fact rather than a misconfiguration. This replaces an earlier version that ran 'zcat /proc/config.gz' with no stderr redirect, which emitted a gzip error and scored CRITICAL on every device where that file is absent.
checks.remediation: MTE cannot be enabled on hardware that lacks it. On ARMv8.5+ devices, enable it for the system or for specific processes via arm64.memtag.bootctl and the per-app memtagMode manifest attribute. Prefer MTE-capable silicon when refreshing fleet hardware.

checks.label: Processes Running as Root
checks.description: Minimize processes running as root
checks.remediation: Identify unnecessary root processes and reconfigure their init.rc entries to run under a dedicated UID.

checks.label: World-Readable Proc Entries
checks.description: Process info readable - normal but review sensitive processes
checks.remediation: Set hidepid=2 on /proc mount to restrict process visibility. Add hidepid=2 to fstab for /proc.

checks.label: Custom Native Daemons
checks.command: ps -A 2>/dev/null | grep -vE 'zygote|system_server|surfaceflinger|android|google|com\.|app_process|dalvikvm' | grep -E '^root|^system' | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq | head -10
checks.description: Non-Android native processes - review for IoT services
checks.remediation: Review each custom daemon. Remove or disable unneeded ones by editing their init.rc service entries.

checks.label: Listening on All Interfaces
checks.command: netstat -tlnp 2>/dev/null | grep '0.0.0.0:' | grep -v '127.0.0.1' || ss -tlnp 2>/dev/null | grep '0.0.0.0:' | head -10
checks.description: Services listening on all interfaces - exposed to network
checks.remediation: Bind services to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0, or use iptables to restrict access to trusted IPs only.

checks.label: Stack Protection Status
checks.description: Stack protection status
checks.remediation: Informational. If stack protection is missing, rebuild binaries with -fstack-protector-strong.

checks.label: Writable Paths in $PATH
checks.command: echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n' | while IFS= read -r d; do [ -n "$d" ] && [ -w "$d" ] && echo "$d"; done
checks.description: Writable dirs in PATH can lead to privilege escalation
checks.remediation: Remove write permissions on PATH directories. Run: chmod o-w <dir> and chmod g-w <dir> for each flagged path.

checks.label: Disable-Verity Property Not Set
checks.description: Disable-verity must not be enabled on locked devices
checks.remediation: Re-enable verity. Run: adb enable-verity, then reboot. Remove persist.sys.disable_verity from build.prop.

checks.label: Battery Saver Mode
checks.description: Battery saver status
checks.remediation: Informational. Toggle battery saver via: adb shell settings put global low_power 0 (or 1 to enable).

checks.label: Doze Mode Enabled
checks.description: Doze mode for battery optimization
checks.remediation: Informational. Enable doze if disabled via: adb shell dumpsys deviceidle enable.

checks.label: Doze Whitelist Apps
checks.description: Apps excluded from doze mode
checks.remediation: Review whitelist and remove unnecessary apps. Run: adb shell dumpsys deviceidle whitelist -<package>.

checks.label: Top 5 Running Processes
checks.description: Initial list of active processes
checks.remediation: Informational. Review the process list for unexpected or unknown entries.

checks.label: bootctl Present
checks.command: command -v bootctl >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo present || echo absent
checks.description: bootctl available to query slot state
checks.remediation: Informational. If absent, A/B slot management is unavailable - verify the device supports A/B updates.

checks.label: Current Slot
checks.description: Device reports current boot slot (a/b or 0/1)
checks.remediation: Informational. If the slot is unexpected, check for failed OTA updates with: bootctl get-suffix.

checks.label: Stock Recovery (No TWRP in PATH)
checks.command: command -v twrp >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo found || echo notfound
checks.description: No custom recovery binary should be present
checks.remediation: Remove the TWRP binary and reflash stock recovery. Run: rm $(which twrp) and flash stock recovery image.

checks.label: Kernel Version
checks.description: Kernel build/version details
checks.remediation: Informational. Record the kernel version and verify it matches the expected vendor release.

checks.label: Audit Logs Enabled
checks.description: Kernel printk log levels (evidence collector)
checks.remediation: Informational. Ensure adequate log levels are set. Adjust with: echo '7 4 1 7' > /proc/sys/kernel/printk.

checks.label: KASLR Enabled
checks.description: Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR) should be enabled to randomize kernel memory layout.
checks.remediation: Enable KASLR by adding 'kaslr' to the kernel command line in the bootloader config, then reboot.

checks.label: NX (No eXecute) Bit Enabled
checks.description: NX bit must be enabled to prevent execution of code in data memory regions.
checks.remediation: Ensure NX/XD is enabled in BIOS/UEFI settings. Rebuild the kernel with PAE support if NX is missing.

checks.label: Core Dumps Disabled
checks.description: Core dumps should be disabled to prevent sensitive data leakage. The sysctl is read with stderr suppressed and reports CORE_PATTERN_UNREADABLE when the node is absent, so a kernel that does not expose it is not failed on absence of evidence. The earlier version ran cat without redirecting stderr, so a missing node put the 'No such file or directory' text into the result, which failed the pattern and scored a finding.
checks.remediation: Disable core dumps. Run: echo '|/dev/null' > /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern. Persist via sysctl.conf.

checks.label: SECCOMP Kernel Support
checks.command: if grep -qi '^Seccomp:' /proc/self/status 2>/dev/null; then M=$(grep -i '^Seccomp:' /proc/self/status 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}'); F=$(grep -i '^Seccomp_filters:' /proc/self/status 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}'); echo "KERNEL_SECCOMP_PRESENT shell_mode=${M:-unknown} shell_filters=${F:-0}"; else echo KERNEL_SECCOMP_ABSENT; fi
checks.description: The kernel exposes a 'Seccomp:' field in /proc/<pid>/status only when CONFIG_SECCOMP is compiled in, so the presence of that field is direct proof of kernel seccomp support and needs no access to /proc/config.gz. Android uses seccomp-bpf to restrict the syscall surface of app processes and of the media and network stacks. The reported shell_mode is the mode of the auditing shell itself (0 disabled, 1 strict, 2 filter) and is expected to be 0, because adb shell is not sandboxed; it is context, not a verdict. This replaces an earlier version that read 'zcat /proc/config.gz' with safe_pattern 'CONFIG_SECCOMP=Y', which could never match because kernel config values are lowercase, and which emitted a gzip error into the result on the majority of devices where /proc/config.gz is absent.
checks.remediation: Rebuild the kernel with CONFIG_SECCOMP=y and CONFIG_SECCOMP_FILTER=y. Android CDD requires seccomp-bpf support; a kernel without it cannot enforce the platform syscall filters.

checks.label: Protected Symlinks Enabled
checks.description: Symlink protection should be enabled to prevent symlink-based privilege escalation. The sysctl is read with stderr suppressed and reports SYSCTL_UNREADABLE when the node is absent, so a kernel that does not expose it is not failed on absence of evidence. The earlier version ran cat without redirecting stderr, so a missing node put the 'No such file or directory' text into the result, which failed the pattern and scored a finding.
checks.remediation: Run: echo 1 > /proc/sys/fs/protected_symlinks. Persist by adding fs.protected_symlinks=1 to sysctl.conf.

checks.label: Protected Hardlinks Enabled
checks.description: Hardlink protection should be enabled to prevent unauthorized file access. The sysctl is read with stderr suppressed and reports SYSCTL_UNREADABLE when the node is absent, so a kernel that does not expose it is not failed on absence of evidence. The earlier version ran cat without redirecting stderr, so a missing node put the 'No such file or directory' text into the result, which failed the pattern and scored a finding.
checks.remediation: Run: echo 1 > /proc/sys/fs/protected_hardlinks. Persist by adding fs.protected_hardlinks=1 to sysctl.conf.

checks.label: Debug Build Type
checks.description: Must be 'user' build. 'userdebug' or 'eng' allow debugging
checks.remediation: Set ro.build.type=user in build.prop and rebuild the system image. Do not ship userdebug or eng builds.

checks.label: Debuggable Flag
checks.description: ro.debuggable=1 allows ptrace, debugging - must be 0
checks.remediation: Set ro.debuggable=0 in build.prop and rebuild the system image.

checks.label: ADB Secure Mode
checks.description: ro.adb.secure=1 requires RSA authentication for ADB
checks.remediation: Set ro.adb.secure=1 in build.prop and rebuild the system image to enforce ADB RSA authentication.

checks.label: ADB Root Access
checks.description: ADB shell should NOT run as root (uid=0)
checks.remediation: Use a user build (ro.build.type=user) which drops ADB to shell user. Run: adb unroot to demote.

checks.label: Default Build Fingerprint
checks.description: Generic/test build fingerprint indicates development firmware
checks.remediation: Rebuild with a proper production fingerprint. Set ro.build.fingerprint to the official release value.

checks.label: Manufacturer Default Unchanged
checks.description: Device model indicates test/development unit
checks.remediation: Flash production firmware. Set ro.product.model to the correct model name in build.prop.

checks.label: Debug Properties Set
checks.description: Debug properties enabled - may leak sensitive info
checks.remediation: Remove debug properties from build.prop. Run: adb shell setprop <debug.property> '' for runtime removal.

checks.label: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)
checks.description: Total packages - FDA requires SBOM for premarket submissions
checks.remediation: Informational. Export the full package list with: pm list packages -f > sbom_packages.txt for SBOM tracking.

checks.label: Third-Party Libraries
checks.description: Shared libraries count - document for SBOM/vulnerability tracking
checks.remediation: Informational. Catalog shared libraries for vulnerability scanning and SBOM documentation.

checks.label: Build Timestamp
checks.description: Firmware build date - document for configuration management
checks.remediation: Informational. Record the build date for audit trails and configuration management.

checks.label: TEE Driver Presence (Present → Info)
checks.description: TEE device nodes found (e.g., /dev/tee*, /dev/trusty*). Presence is informational.
checks.remediation: Informational. Verify TEE is functional by checking keymaster/gatekeeper HAL status.

checks.label: TEE Vendor Prop (Empty → Verify)
checks.description: Empty output is common (vendors often hide TEE props); flag for manual verify.
checks.remediation: Manually verify TEE functionality by testing hardware-backed keystore operations.

checks.label: TPM Keystore Presence
checks.description: Checks for hardware-backed keystore modules
checks.remediation: Ensure a hardware-backed keystore HAL is present. Install the vendor-specific keystore module if missing.

checks.label: Auto Time Enabled
checks.description: Auto time sync helps prevent cert/token attacks
checks.remediation: Enable auto time sync. Run: adb shell settings put global auto_time 1.

checks.label: Auto Timezone
checks.description: Automatic timezone detection
checks.remediation: Enable auto timezone. Run: adb shell settings put global auto_time_zone 1.

checks.label: NTP Server
checks.description: Configured NTP server for time sync
checks.remediation: Set a trusted NTP server. Run: adb shell settings put global ntp_server time.google.com.

checks.label: Time Zone
checks.description: Current timezone setting
checks.remediation: Set the correct timezone. Run: adb shell setprop persist.sys.timezone <Region/City>.

checks.label: WebView Provider
checks.description: WebView implementation provider
checks.remediation: Set an official WebView provider. Run: adb shell settings put global webview_provider com.google.android.webview.

checks.label: WebView Version
checks.command: dumpsys package com.google.android.webview 2>/dev/null | grep versionName | head -1
checks.description: WebView version - should be updated
checks.remediation: Update WebView via Play Store or sideload the latest APK: pm install -r <webview.apk>.

checks.label: Safe Boot Disallowed
checks.description: safe_boot_disallowed controls whether the device may be rebooted into Safe Boot. Note: this is unrelated to WebView SafeBrowsing (see separate check). Informational; the value indicates whether OEM or admin policy restricts Safe Boot access.
checks.remediation: Informational. Review safe boot policy settings in your device management configuration.

checks.label: Emulator Detection (QEMU)
checks.description: QEMU emulator property set - POS and IoT devices must run on physical hardware, not emulators
checks.remediation: Deploy on physical hardware only. If testing, remove ro.kernel.qemu property from build.prop.

checks.label: Virtual Hardware Detection
checks.description: Virtual/emulated hardware detected - goldfish/ranchu=Android emulator, vbox=VirtualBox
checks.remediation: Deploy on physical hardware. Virtual environments are not suitable for production POS/IoT devices.

checks.label: System Memory Status
checks.description: System memory baseline - abnormally low available memory may indicate memory scraping attacks or crypto mining
checks.remediation: Informational. Investigate if available memory is abnormally low - check for rogue processes with top or ps.

checks.label: Suspicious Executables in /data/local/tmp
checks.description: Executable files in /data/local/tmp - common staging location for exploits, Frida gadgets, and malware payloads
checks.remediation: Remove all executables. Run: adb shell rm /data/local/tmp/<filename> for each flagged file.

checks.label: SIM Card / Cellular Status
checks.description: SIM card state - POS terminals and IoT kiosks typically should not have active cellular connectivity
checks.remediation: If cellular is not required, disable the radio. Run: adb shell settings put global airplane_mode_on 1.

checks.label: High CPU Usage Processes
checks.description: Processes using >50% CPU - may indicate crypto miners or RAM scrapers
checks.remediation: Identify and kill suspicious high-CPU processes. Run: kill <pid>. Investigate and remove the binary.

checks.label: System Packages Total Count
checks.description: Total system package count (typical: 80-250) - compare against device baseline for tampering
checks.remediation: Compare count against a known-good baseline. Investigate discrepancies with: pm list packages -s.

checks.label: Process Memory Maps Count
checks.description: Running process count via maps - baseline for anomaly detection (typical: 50-200)
checks.remediation: Compare against a known baseline. If count is abnormally high, investigate unknown processes with ps -A.

checks.label: SECCOMP Status of Init (PID 1)
checks.description: SECCOMP mode of init process: 0=disabled, 1=strict, 2=filter (BPF). Mode 2 indicates SECCOMP-BPF syscall filtering is active.
checks.remediation: Informational. SECCOMP mode 2 (filter) is expected on hardened Android systems.

checks.label: SECCOMP Status of Zygote
checks.command: pid=$(pidof zygote 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $1}'); [ -n "$pid" ] && cat /proc/$pid/status 2>/dev/null | grep Seccomp || echo 'zygote_not_found'
checks.description: Zygote is the parent of all Android app processes. SECCOMP filter mode 2 on Zygote ensures all spawned apps inherit syscall filtering.
checks.remediation: SECCOMP mode 2 on Zygote is required for Android app sandbox. Verify seccomp_bpf is enabled in Android init.

checks.label: Qualcomm QSEE TEE Device Node
checks.description: Qualcomm Secure Execution Environment (QSEE) device node. Presence confirms Qualcomm TrustZone TEE is active on this device.
checks.remediation: Informational. QSEE is the Qualcomm TEE implementation. Ensure QSEE is running and not exploitable via CVE-2015-6639 / CVE-2016-2431.

checks.label: Qualcomm TEE (QTEE) Properties
checks.description: Qualcomm TEE (QTEE/QSEE) system properties. Indicates Qualcomm TrustZone-based security services are active.
checks.remediation: Informational. Verify Qualcomm security patches are applied for TEE-related CVEs.

checks.label: MediaTek Mobicore TEE Device Node
checks.description: MediaTek Mobicore (t-base) TEE device nodes. Presence confirms MediaTek TrustZone TEE is active. Used on MTK and some Samsung Exynos devices.
checks.remediation: Informational. Apply Mobicore/t-base TEE security patches from MediaTek. Verify no known Mobicore CVEs are unpatched.

checks.label: Samsung TEEGRIS TEE Detection
checks.description: Samsung TEEGRIS is Samsung's proprietary TrustZone OS replacing Mobicore on Exynos 9810+ devices. Provides hardware-backed security services.
checks.remediation: Informational. TEEGRIS is Samsung's TEE on newer Exynos devices. Ensure Knox/TEE patches are applied.

checks.label: Google Trusty TEE Device Node
checks.description: Google Trusty TEE IPC device node. Trusty is Google's open-source TrustZone OS used in Android reference hardware and some OEM devices.
checks.remediation: Informational. Trusty TEE presence confirms Google-managed TrustZone environment.

checks.label: Trusty TEE Properties
checks.description: Google Trusty TEE system properties. Indicates Trusty TrustZone OS is active as the TEE implementation.
checks.remediation: Informational. Verify Trusty version is up to date with Android security patches.

checks.label: Hardware Gatekeeper HAL
checks.description: Hardware Gatekeeper HAL must be present for TEE-backed password/PIN authentication. Software fallback gatekeeper is weaker.
checks.remediation: Ensure hardware-backed gatekeeper HAL is present and not falling back to software implementation.

checks.label: KASLR (Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization)
checks.description: If /proc/kallsyms returns non-zero addresses, KASLR may not be fully effective or the process has CAP_SYSLOG. Zero addresses confirm KASLR is masking kernel symbols.
checks.remediation: Ensure kernel is compiled with CONFIG_RANDOMIZE_BASE=y and restrict /proc/kallsyms to root via CONFIG_KALLSYMS_ALL=n.

checks.label: Device Provisioned (Setup Wizard Complete)
checks.description: device_provisioned indicates whether initial device setup completed. A value of 0 means the device is stuck in (or has been reset into) the setup wizard, which is a partially-configured state often with weaker defaults. Critical for kiosk and POS deployments to confirm post-provisioning state.
checks.remediation: Complete the device setup flow. If the value is 0 unexpectedly, the device may have been factory reset; reprovision through the standard onboarding.

checks.label: WebView SafeBrowsing Enabled
checks.description: WebView SafeBrowsing protects in-app web content from malicious URLs (similar to Chrome SafeBrowsing). Null or empty means the per-device override is unset and WebView uses its own default (typically enabled). Explicit 0 means an admin or app has disabled it.
checks.remediation: If the value is 0, restore WebView default by clearing the setting: 'settings delete global webview_safe_browsing_state'.

checks.label: io_uring Restriction (kernel 6.6+)
checks.description: io_uring has been one of the most productive Linux kernel exploitation surfaces of recent years (a large share of kernel LPE bugs and exploit-competition wins). Android restricts it two ways: seccomp blocks it for untrusted apps, and GKI 6.6+ kernels expose the kernel.io_uring_disabled sysctl. 2 = io_uring disabled for everyone (strongest). 1 = restricted to privileged processes (Android's hardened default on kernels that ship the knob). 0 = unrestricted, which needlessly re-opens a major kernel attack surface and fails this check. NO_SYSCTL = the kernel predates the knob (5.x GKI); those builds rely on seccomp alone and are reported as acceptable rather than failing, since the sysctl simply does not exist there.
checks.remediation: If the value is 0, restore the restriction: 'echo 2 > /proc/sys/kernel/io_uring_disabled' (root), and fix whatever init/vendor script relaxed it so the setting survives reboot. Value 1 or 2 is expected stock posture on Android 15+ devices with 6.6+ kernels.

checks.label: 16KB Page Size Build
checks.command: V=$(getprop ro.product.build.16k_page.enabled 2>/dev/null); P=$(getconf PAGE_SIZE 2>/dev/null); echo "16k_build=${V:-unset} page_size=${P:-unknown}"
checks.description: Android 15+ supports 16KB memory pages (and Android 16+ requires new device support for it on arm64). Larger pages are primarily a performance feature, but they also perturb heap-grooming and page-spray assumptions baked into many public kernel and userspace exploits, so recording the page size is useful audit context when assessing exploit exposure. Reports the 16KB build property and the runtime PAGE_SIZE (4096 or 16384). Informational only: 4KB remains a fully supported, secure configuration.
checks.remediation: Nothing to fix. When refreshing fleet hardware, note that Android 16+ launch devices increasingly ship 16KB-page kernels, and in-house native code (JNI .so files) must be rebuilt with 16KB-aligned ELF segments to run on them.

checks.label: Heap Allocator Hardening (Scudo / GWP-ASan)
checks.command: SDK=$(getprop ro.build.version.sdk 2>/dev/null); if [ -z "$SDK" ]; then echo SDK_UNKNOWN; elif [ "$SDK" -lt 30 ] 2>/dev/null; then echo "PRE_SCUDO_SDK_$SDK"; else G=$(getprop 2>/dev/null | grep -c 'libc.debug.gwp_asan'); M=$(getprop libc.debug.malloc.options 2>/dev/null); echo "SCUDO_DEFAULT sdk=$SDK gwp_asan_props=$G malloc_options=${M:-unset}"; fi
checks.description: Android 11 (API 30) made Scudo the default native heap allocator for all platform and app processes. Scudo adds chunk header checksums, delayed free lists, and randomised allocation that turn many heap overflow and use-after-free bugs into aborts instead of exploitable corruption. GWP-ASan samples a small fraction of allocations for guarded pages on top of it. Setting libc.debug.malloc.options switches processes to the debug allocator, which disables the hardened paths, so it should be unset on any production build. Builds below API 30 report PRE_SCUDO_SDK_<n> and use the older jemalloc path with none of these protections.
checks.remediation: Clear the debug allocator property with 'setprop libc.debug.malloc.options ""' and confirm no init script or build overlay sets it. For builds below API 30, the only fix is an OS upgrade: the allocator cannot be replaced in place.
checks.why: Scudo converts a large class of heap corruption primitives into controlled aborts. Reverting to the debug allocator removes that mitigation process-wide.
checks.risk_if_fail: Heap overflows and use-after-free bugs in native code become exploitable instead of aborting.

checks.label: GKI Kernel and Module Loading Restriction
checks.command: K=$(uname -r 2>/dev/null); if echo "$K" | grep -qE '\-android[0-9]+'; then G=GKI; else G=NON_GKI; fi; MD=$(cat /proc/sys/kernel/modules_disabled 2>/dev/null); echo "kernel=${K:-unknown} type=$G modules_disabled=${MD:-unreadable}"
checks.description: Reports the kernel release string, whether it is a Generic Kernel Image build (GKI releases carry an -androidNN- suffix and receive Android security patches directly from Google rather than waiting on an SoC vendor backport), and the state of the kernel.modules_disabled sysctl. When modules_disabled is 1 the kernel refuses all further module loads for the rest of the boot, which closes the most direct path from a root shell to persistent kernel-level code. Reported for review rather than as a failure because most Android devices legitimately leave the sysctl at 0 to support late-loading vendor modules, and a NON_GKI kernel is normal on older or heavily customised platforms.
checks.remediation: Prefer GKI-based kernels so security patches arrive on the Android bulletin cadence instead of the SoC vendor cadence. On locked-down appliance builds where every module is loaded during early boot, set kernel.modules_disabled to 1 once boot completes to block later module loads.

checks.label: Unprivileged eBPF Disabled
checks.description: kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled controls whether an unprivileged process may load eBPF programs. 0 permits it, 1 disables it permanently for the boot, 2 disables it but allows a privileged process to re-enable. Unprivileged eBPF has produced a long run of local privilege escalations because the verifier is a large attack surface reachable without any capability. Either 1 or 2 is acceptable. SYSCTL_ABSENT is treated as passing because a kernel built without eBPF does not expose the node and must not be failed for absence of evidence.
checks.remediation: Set kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled to 1 in the device sysctl configuration, or build the kernel with CONFIG_BPF_UNPRIV_DEFAULT_OFF=y so the restriction survives reboot.
checks.why: The eBPF verifier is reachable from an unprivileged process and has repeatedly been the root of local privilege escalation.
checks.risk_if_fail: Any local process or app can load eBPF programs, reaching a kernel attack surface that should require privilege.

checks.label: SUID Core Dumps Restricted
checks.description: fs.suid_dumpable controls whether a setuid process may produce a core dump. 0 never dumps, 2 dumps but the file is readable only by root, and 1 dumps with normal ownership, which lets an unprivileged user read the memory image of a privileged process. Only 1 is dangerous, so both 0 and 2 pass.
checks.remediation: Set fs.suid_dumpable to 0, or to 2 if crash collection from privileged processes is required.
checks.why: A dumpable setuid process writes its memory, including any secrets it holds, to a file an unprivileged user can read.
checks.risk_if_fail: Credentials and keys held by privileged processes can be recovered from core dumps by any local user.

checks.label: Protected FIFOs Enabled
checks.description: fs.protected_fifos stops a process from opening a FIFO it does not own inside a world-writable sticky directory, closing a class of attack where a privileged process is tricked into writing to an attacker-controlled pipe placed in a shared temp directory. 1 protects FIFOs in world-writable sticky directories, 2 extends that to group-writable ones. This complements the protected_symlinks and protected_hardlinks checks already present.
checks.remediation: Set fs.protected_fifos to 2 in the device sysctl configuration.
checks.why: Without it, an attacker can plant a FIFO in a shared temp directory and block or redirect a privileged writer.
checks.risk_if_fail: A privileged process can be induced to write into an attacker-controlled pipe.

checks.label: Protected Regular Files Enabled
checks.description: fs.protected_regular is the regular-file counterpart of protected_fifos: it prevents a process from opening a regular file it does not own for writing inside a world-writable sticky directory. It closes the file-squatting variant of the shared temp directory attack, where an attacker pre-creates a filename a privileged process is about to write.
checks.remediation: Set fs.protected_regular to 2 in the device sysctl configuration.
checks.why: Pre-creating a file in a shared directory redirects a privileged writer into a file the attacker controls.
checks.risk_if_fail: A privileged process can be induced to write into an attacker-owned file.

checks.label: Magic SysRq Key Configuration
checks.description: kernel.sysrq is a bitmask controlling the magic SysRq key, which can dump kernel memory and register state, kill processes, remount filesystems and reboot the device from a physical key combination or by writing to /proc/sysrq-trigger. 0 disables it entirely and is the hardened setting for an appliance. Reported for review rather than as a failure because production Android builds and desktop Linux ship very different defaults (0 versus 176), so a fixed pass value would produce a finding on one platform or the other regardless of the real posture.
checks.remediation: On a kiosk, POS or appliance build with any physical access exposure, set kernel.sysrq to 0. Where debugging access is genuinely needed, restrict the bitmask to the specific functions required rather than leaving it fully enabled.

checks.label: Panic On Oops
checks.description: kernel.panic_on_oops makes the kernel panic rather than continue after an oops. Continuing after an oops leaves the kernel in an undefined state that an exploit can work with, so 1 is the hardened setting and is what Android sets on many production builds. Reported for review because the value legitimately differs between production and engineering builds and between platforms, so failing on a fixed value would misreport one of them.
checks.remediation: Set kernel.panic_on_oops to 1 on production builds so a kernel fault halts the device instead of leaving it running in an inconsistent state.

checks.label: SGID Binaries Inventory
checks.description: Lists set-group-ID binaries on the read-only system partitions. Android ships very few, so the list should be short and stable across builds of the same firmware. An SGID binary runs with the group of its owner regardless of who invokes it, so an unexpected entry is a privilege boundary worth examining. Reported as an inventory rather than pass or fail because a small set of legitimate SGID binaries is normal and the exact set is OEM-specific. The companion SUID Binaries check covers the set-user-ID case; nothing covered SGID before.
checks.remediation: Compare the list against the same firmware build on a known-good device. Investigate any binary that is not part of the stock image, and remove the SGID bit from anything that does not require it.

checks.label: World-Writable Executables On System Partitions
checks.description: Finds files on the read-only system partitions that are both world-writable and executable. On a healthy device this must return nothing: the system partitions are mounted read-only and no stock binary carries write permission for other. A hit means either the partition has been remounted read-write and modified, or the image was built with broken permissions, and in both cases any local process can replace the contents of a binary that other processes execute.
checks.remediation: Remove write permission with 'chmod o-w' on each file listed, confirm the partition is mounted read-only, and treat the device as potentially tampered with until the image is verified against the stock build.
checks.why: A world-writable executable on a system partition lets any local process replace code that privileged processes run.
checks.risk_if_fail: Arbitrary code execution in the context of whatever process invokes the modified binary.

checks.label: Kernel Tracing Interface Not World-Accessible
checks.command: D=''; for p in /sys/kernel/tracing /sys/kernel/debug/tracing; do [ -d "$p" ] && D="$D $p:$(ls -ld $p 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $1}')"; done; [ -z "$D" ] && echo NO_TRACEFS || { echo "$D" | grep -qE ':d[rwx-]{6}r|:d[rwx-]{6}[rwx-]{2}[rwx]' && echo "TRACEFS_WORLD_ACCESSIBLE$D" || echo "TRACEFS_RESTRICTED$D"; }
checks.description: tracefs exposes ftrace, kprobes and the kernel trace buffer. When readable by an unprivileged process it leaks kernel pointers and timing that defeat KASLR, and when writable it allows arbitrary kernel tracing. Production Android should either not mount it or keep it root-only. NO_TRACEFS is treated as passing because a kernel built without ftrace is the strongest outcome and must not be failed for absence of evidence.
checks.remediation: Unmount tracefs on production builds, or restrict it to root with mode 0700. Confirm no init script mounts /sys/kernel/debug with permissive modes.
checks.why: Readable tracefs leaks kernel addresses and timing, which is the information an exploit needs to defeat KASLR.
checks.risk_if_fail: An unprivileged process can read kernel pointers and trace kernel execution.

checks.label: procfs hidepid Setting
checks.description: Reports the mount options on /proc, in particular whether hidepid is set. Without hidepid any process can enumerate every other process, read its command line and environment, and observe its memory maps, which is a reconnaissance primitive for local privilege escalation. Android relies on SELinux and per-app UIDs rather than hidepid, so its absence is the platform norm and not by itself a finding, which is why this is reported for review rather than failed.
checks.remediation: On a hardened appliance build, mount /proc with hidepid=2 and a suitable gid so processes cannot enumerate one another. On stock Android, verify SELinux is enforcing instead, since that is the control the platform actually relies on.

checks.label: Native Daemon Capability Sets
checks.command: for p in 1 $(ls /proc 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^[0-9]+$' | head -40); do n=$(cat /proc/$p/comm 2>/dev/null); e=$(grep -m1 '^CapEff' /proc/$p/status 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}'); [ -n "$e" ] && [ "$e" != "0000000000000000" ] && echo "$n $e"; done | sort -u | head -20
checks.description: Lists running processes that hold a non-empty effective capability set, with the capability bitmask. SELinux confines what a domain may do, but capabilities decide what the kernel will let a process attempt in the first place, and a daemon holding CAP_SYS_ADMIN or CAP_SYS_PTRACE remains dangerous even under a tight policy. A full bitmask of 0000001fffffffff indicates all capabilities. Reported as an inventory for review because the legitimate set is entirely build-specific, and capped at 40 processes so the sweep stays bounded.
checks.remediation: For each daemon listed, check the capability set against what it actually needs and drop the rest in its init service definition. CAP_SYS_ADMIN on a vendor daemon is worth particular scrutiny since it is close to full root.

checks.label: Registered Binder Service Inventory
checks.command: S=$(service list 2>/dev/null | grep -c ':'); V=$(service list 2>/dev/null | grep -ciE 'vendor|oem|qti|mtk|samsung|huawei'); [ "${S:-0}" = "0" ] && echo NO_SERVICE_LIST || echo "binder_services=$S vendor_services=$V"
checks.description: Counts the services registered with servicemanager and how many carry a vendor or OEM prefix. Every registered binder service is an IPC entry point reachable by any process the SELinux policy allows to find it, and vendor services are the ones least likely to have had the scrutiny the AOSP framework services get. This provides the attack-surface inventory count that a Binder-focused review starts from. Informational: the count is build-specific and a high number is normal on an OEM device.
checks.remediation: Enumerate the vendor services with 'service list' and review each for exposed transactions that do not check the caller UID or permission. Remove services that are not needed on a production build.
